extracted.intended_audience: USCIS/Department of Homeland Security staff, immigration attorneys, bond obligors/co-obligors, immigrants, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_short: public charge bond cancellation and breach
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed regulatory standards and procedures governing when a public charge bond is canceled or deemed breached, how requests are submitted and adjudicated, evidentiary burdens, appeals, remedies, and processing fees. Covers definitions (e.g., permanent departure), required forms, exceptions, disclosure, and collection practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bond termination events
rubrics_metrics.description: INA section 213 requires that a public charge bond 'terminate upon the permanent departure from the United States, the naturalization, or the death of such alien.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reiterates statutory termination events (naturalization/citizenship, permanent departure, death) and notes return of sums except to extent forfeited for violation. (See INA section 213, 8 U.S.C. 1183.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'permanent departure' for bond cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent departure for purposes of canceling a public charge bond means that the alien has left the United States on a lasting, non-temporary basis after losing the lawful permanent resident status either voluntarily or involuntarily, and is physically outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes that both elements must be established: (1) lost or abandoned LPR status (involuntary loss only in removal proceedings with a final order or through rescission of adjustment), and (2) physical departure from the U.S. Determination of abandonment is fact-specific (length of absence, ties, property, residence, intent/actions). If loss occurs by operation of law, alien must submit evidence of official determination (e.g., removal order). Citations to case law (Matter of Huang, Kane, Quijencio, Castro, Montero) illustrate factors considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of voluntary relinquishment via Form I-407
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien may demonstrate voluntary relinquishment of lawful permanent resident status for purposes of bond cancellation only by showing proof that he or she has submitted Form I-407 to the U.S. Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes requiring Form I-407 filing to ensure consistent adjudication and to avoid having officers determine intent. Form I-407 creates a record and confirms voluntary, informed waiver of rights; the form would not have a fee. Even if filed, the declaration is not necessarily dispositive in removal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation after five years of LPR status
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to continue to cancel a public charge bond after the fifth anniversary of admission as an immigrant, provided that the alien files a request to cancel the bond and the alien did not become a public charge prior to the fifth anniversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tracks existing 8 CFR 103.6(c)(1). The five-year window reflects related statutory timeframes (e.g., deportation liability under INA §237(a)(5), PRWORA limits). The alien must file Form I-356 and satisfy that no public benefits (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b)) were received prior to the fifth anniversary and that bond conditions were not violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: No retained discretionary cancellation for 'not likely to become public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to not retain the discretion to cancel a public charge bond at any time on the ground that the immigrant is 'not likely to become a public charge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains rationale: many aliens who adjust status will not have a second public charge determination; Congress selected five years in related contexts; retaining bond for at least five years ensures ability to recoup costs. This is a policy limitation on preexisting discretionary cancellation authority (8 CFR 103.6(c)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation when alien obtains status exempt from public charge grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS would cancel the public charge bond if an alien subject to a public charge bond obtains an immigration status while present in the United States that is exempt from public charge grounds of inadmissibility (as listed in 8 CFR 212.23), following the initial grant of LPR status, provided a request for cancellation is filed and the alien has not breached the bond conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asylum or other exempt status. DHS notes that retaining the bond in such situations 'no longer serves the intended purpose' because the purpose is to ensure the alien does not become a public charge. If no cancellation request is filed, the bond remains in effect. If the alien later adjusts to a status subject to public charge inadmissibility, DHS may reassess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-356 and evidence requirements for cancellation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to cancel the bond must be submitted on the form designated by DHS (proposed Form I-356), in accordance with instructions, and with any mandatory fee (proposed $25). The request must include evidence of naturalization, permanent departure, or a death certificate (if deceased), and information regarding receipt of public benefits as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because USCIS typically lacks information about naturalization or departure, the alien must submit supporting documentation. Any information collected will comply with privacy laws. If information is insufficient, USCIS may request additional information under 8 CFR part 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for cancellation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligor and the alien have the burden to establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the conditions for cancellation of the public charge bond have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If USCIS finds the information insufficient, it may request additional evidence in accordance with 8 CFR part 103. This allocates the evidentiary burden to the parties seeking cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return of funds and release upon cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS determines that cancellation is warranted, USCIS would notify the obligor and return the full value of any cash or cash equivalent deposited by the obligor to secure the bond plus interest; upon cancellation the obligor would be released from liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows current practice and proposed 8 CFR 213.1. If denied, USCIS will notify obligor of reasons and right to appeal under 8 CFR part 103, subpart A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights and process for obligors (cancellation or breach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond obligor may appeal a denial to cancel the bond or a breach determination to the Administrative Appeals Office (AAO) by filing Notice of Appeal or Motion (Form I-290B) with the appropriate fee and evidence; under the proposal, an obligor may only file a motion after an unfavorable AAO decision on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational efficiency: the officer rendering the initial decision must review the initial decision per 8 CFR 103.3(a)(2); if the officer agrees favorable action is warranted, they may treat appeal as a motion and enter a favorable decision. The alien cannot appeal because the bond contract is between the obligor and the U.S. government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bond breach (receipt of public benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond would be considered breached if the alien has received public benefits, as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b), after the alien's adjustment of status to that of a lawful permanent resident and until the public charge bond is cancelled under 8 CFR 213.1(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with other proposed provisions, benefits received while the alien is in a status exempt from the public charge ground (8 CFR 212.23) following initial grant of LPR status would not be considered. DHS also would not consider certain military-related benefits or benefits received after naturalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach for other conditions imposed as part of the bond
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond would be considered breached if any other condition imposed by USCIS as part of the public charge bond is breached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognizes that public charge bonds may contain additional specific conditions; breach of those conditions (not just receipt of public benefits) can trigger breach findings. Proposed citations: 8 CFR 213.1(d) and (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 'substantial violation' standard and replacement with public charge/benefits definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes not to retain the phrase 'substantial violation' (used in 8 CFR 103.6 generally) in the public charge bond provision; instead DHS would incorporate principles that govern the public charge and public benefits definitions at proposed 8 CFR 212.21(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public charge bonds have been distinguished from other immigration bonds; the proposed approach defines breach by reference to receipt of public benefits after adjustment or breach of other bond conditions (see Matter of Viado).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure, evidentiary development, and obligor response during breach adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS learns of a breach, it would disclose such information to the obligor to the extent permitted by law, may request additional information from the benefits-granting agency or from the alien/obligor if information is insufficient, and would provide the obligor an opportunity to respond and submit rebuttal evidence with a specified deadline. A copy of any notification to the obligor regarding the breach would also be sent to the alien and the alien's representative (if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS may learn of benefit receipt via agency notification or as part of a cancellation request. The process follows 8 CFR part 103 procedures for requests for additional information and for providing responses/rebuttal by obligors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach decision finality, reopening, and effects of non-appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: After obligor response or the response deadline, USCIS makes a breach determination and informs obligor of appeal rights; if the appeals period to the AAO expires or obligor fails to appeal, the breach determination becomes administratively final and USCIS would issue a demand for payment (if a surety bond) pursuant to 31 CFR 901.2. USCIS may reopen a breach determination at any time pursuant to 8 CFR 103.5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations on when motions may be filed (only after AAO unfavorable decision) are proposed for operational efficiency. Denial of a motion can be appealed to AAO; agency practice re: tolling appeals is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy upon breach: collection as liquidated damages
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS determines that the bond has been breached, DHS proposes that USCIS would collect on the bond in full, meaning the total monetary amount of the bond as liquidated damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This departs from legacy INS Operating Instructions that contemplated forfeiture only of the amount of public benefits received. DHS explains total damages to government go beyond the benefits amount and are difficult to calculate precisely; liquidated damages are presented as an appropriate remedy and supported by case law and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of administrative remedies before judicial action
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must first exhaust all administrative remedies and obtain a final decision from USCIS in accordance with 8 CFR part 103 before being able to bring suit challenging USCIS cancellation or bond breach determination in Federal district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts review bond breach determinations under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) framework. DHS invites public comments on bond type, amount, duration, substitution, cancellation, and other aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing fees for public charge bonds and cancellation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to charge $25 for the posting of a public charge bond, $25 for the posting of a substitute public charge bond, and $25 when the alien, obligor or co-obligor requests to cancel the public charge bond (i.e., when Form I-356 is filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INA section 286(m), 8 U.S.C. 1356(m), authorizes DHS to set fees to ensure recovery of full costs of adjudication and related services.
